evening.title: Electric car sales nearly double in October
evening.text: New Delhi: Sales of electric cars in the Indian market almost doubled to 35,777 units last month from a year earlier, according to vehicle registration data from the government’s Vahan portal, indicating an increasing shift among consumers to electric amid high fuel prices.EV sales were 18,055 in the same month last year, as per vehicle registration data from the portal.EVs accounted for about 7% of total passenger vehicle sales in October, compared with 3.2% a year earlier.While the increase in fuel prices due to geopolitical tensions has been accelerating a customer shift to electric vehicles during most of the ongoing calendar year, the sales also got additional support from the improving charging infrastructure and the launch of models across price points.Tata Motors retained its lead in the EV market with a 40.7% share in October. Mahindra had a 23.7% share, followed by JSW MG Motor India (16.4), VinFast (7.2) and Maruti Suzuki (3.3%).Electric car registrations in the first 10 months of the calendar year totalled 287,453 units, already exceeding the sales volume of 176,817 units in the entire 2025 by a large margin.Among other established brands, Kia’s EV sales more than doubled, powered by demand for the Syros EV. At Korean auto major Hyundai, sales of electric cars rose 70% to 753 units in October. Chinese brand BYD's sales rose 29% to 735 units last month, but its market share declined to 2% from 3% a year earlier. Toyota Kirloskar Motor reported 189 EV registrations last month, and Stellantis 60 registrations.Tata and Mahindra together accounted for about two out of every three electric cars sold in the local market with a combined segment share of 64.4% in October. Their combined share a year earlier was about 62%.

evening.title: Exercise Garud Shakti Sees India, Indonesia Practise Combat Tracking
evening.text:
In yet another step towards strengthening defence cooperation, the armies of India and Indonesia undertook simulated combat tracking exercises in jungle terrain on Saturday, as part of ongoing joint military exercise ‘Garud Shakti 2026’ in Banyuwangi.
In a post on X, the Indian Embassy in Jakarta said the training focused on tracking and pursuing targets through specialised reading of the ground.
The exercise also familiarised the elite forces of the Indian Army and the Indonesian Army (TNI-AD) with the operational use of drones for surveillance, reconnaissance and situational awareness in dense jungle environments, combining traditional fieldcraft with specialised technologies.
“The art of ‘reading’ the jungle and ‘mastering’ the skies. Following the gains of Day 5, Special Forces of the Indian Army and TNI-AD undertook simulated combat tracking training in jungle terrain, aimed at pursuing a target’s trail by specialised reading of the ground. Troops also received training on operational employment of drones for surveillance, reconnaissance and situational awareness in dense jungles,” the Indian Embassy said.
“Effectively Day 6 exposed the elite forces to traditional fieldcraft and niche technologies, thus ensuring that no trail goes cold and no threat is left unaddressed,” it added.
According to the Indian mission, the special forces of the Indian Army and TNI-AD also undertook patrolling drills in jungle terrain, building on the earlier slithering training.
“Troops rehearsed the full sequence of heli-borne operations, from rapid insertion to securing the landing zone, tactical patrolling and mission execution in a dense jungle terrain. These drills are aimed at building trust and confidence in each other’s tactics, techniques and procedures, while providing an opportunity to exchange best practices,” it posted on X.
Earlier on Thursday, Special Forces personnel from India and Indonesia participated in live-fire training in Banyuwangi to hone their combat skills through marksmanship drills, sniper firing and rapid transition fire on the move, embodying the ethos of “One Shot. One Kill.”
“These tactical-level engagements sharpen individual skill, strengthen interoperability and bolster joint readiness, laying the foundation for deeper strategic collaboration in our collaboration against terrorism of all forms. Sharper skills. Seamless interoperability. United against terror,” the Indian Embassy stated.
The India-Indonesia Joint Special Forces Exercise Garuda Shakti commenced at Banyuwangi in Indonesia on Tuesday, with the Special Forces of the two nations set to train together in jungle warfare operations until November 6, the Ministry of Defence said.
The Indian contingent comprises troops from the Parachute Regiment (Special Forces), while the Indonesian side is represented by personnel from the Indonesian Special Forces.
“The exercise aims to strengthen mutual understanding, cooperation and interoperability between the Special Forces of the two nations. The training focuses on tactics, techniques and procedures for special operations in jungle environments, including obstacle crossing, combat marksmanship, mountaineering, air assault training and combat-hardening sessions,” the Ministry stated.
Source: IANS

evening.title: Armenian Army Seen Using Indian-Made Zen Weapons Simulator
evening.text:
New footage from Armenia’s Ministry of Defence appears to show the Indian-made Advanced Weapons Simulator (AWeSim), developed by Hyderabad-based Zen Technologies, being used by the Armenian military — showcasing another example of India’s increasing footprint in defence training technology globally.
The AWeSim can be used to simulate small arms scenarios enabling users to practice handling, shooting and targeting weapons in a controlled environment. It can be set up to simulate training on numerous different types of firearms and can be used to train new recruits, commandos and special forces, according to Zen Technologies.
The fact that it features within Armenian military footage shows how India’s defence relationship with Armenian has moved into the training space as well as traditional weapons and ammunitions.
The company announced in October 2023 that they had approved the opening of a branch office in Armenia, to boost business development and sales alongside service and support.
Armenian state news agency Armenpress reported in November 2023 that Armenia had signed a contract with Zen Technologies for around US$41.5 million for an anti-drone system and training package. This is not necessarily the confirmed value of AWeSim however, it was for the total contract value. Zen Technologies are well known for their counter unmanned aircraft systems, but are also a major player in the military simulation space, offering infantry weaponry, mortar, anti tank guided missile, air defence gun and armoured vehicle simulators.
These systems can improve training opportunities for armed forces, reduce the amount of ammunition used, reduce wear and tear on equipment and reduce costs. They can also help instructors evaluate their trainees.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: Indian Army Explores Autonomous UGVs and UAVs for Future Warfare
evening.text:
The Indian Army’s Armoured Corps are looking to increase the connectivity and autonomy of the battlefield through the development of a Manned-Unmanned Teaming (MUM-T) system. The system will see Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs), Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and a Command and Control Station integrated together to improve the reach of armoured vehicles whilst protecting the crew.
The UGV is expected to be at the core of the UGV fleet with a 500-1000kg payload capability. It should also be able to carry any weaponry, intelligence gathering equipment, communications equipment and other payloads needed for the mission. The vehicle should be able to travel at a speed of 30-40km/h on roads to accompany armoured vehicles.
The UGV is expected to have around 10-12 hours of endurance when operating in a hybrid configuration. A high level of autonomy is expected with the UGV having autonomous navigation, SLAM, obstacle avoidance and secure communications.
SLAM will help with creating a map of the area the UGV is in, whilst helping to locate the vehicle. If the UGV can navigate autonomously and detect obstacles it can be used in complex environments. The UGV is expected to be multi-role with the potential to have a Remote Weapon Station, Medium Machine Gun or Anti-tank Guided Missiles fitted. This means the UGV could provide extra firepower.
This could prove useful for high risk reconnaissance missions. The armed UGV could be sent forward to investigate enemy positions, whilst observing defences. This would keep the soldier further away from danger. The UGV is expected to have payloads for Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance. With electro optical, IR, Thermal Imaging and Lidar the UGV would have great observation capabilities, day or night. Combined with autonomous navigation the vehicle would be able to identify targets.
UGVs could also be used with UAVs. The UGV could be used as a forward node for small UAVs and loitering munitions. This means the UGV can carry, launch or support small UAVs. This gives the armoured vehicles some extra reach for sensing.
The Command and Control Station will give the human element to the MUM-T system. The idea is to give the soldier the ability to control, monitor and allocate missions to the various unmanned platforms. In the future this could mean just one operator or small group could control multiple unmanned platforms depending on how autonomous they are. The system would allow the UAVs and UGVs to share their sensor information to give a common picture of the battlefield.
This could revolutionise how reconnaissance, clearing, surveillance and engagement missions are carried out by the Armoured Corps. Instead of using just manned vehicles to go into dangerous areas, unmanned vehicles could be sent forward to identify threats.
Hybrid propulsion is an important aspect here, meaning the Army are looking to use something that can be used for a long period of time in the field. However, to ensure the UGV has enough endurance to carry a large payload some optimisation will need to take place with power generation, battery size, thermal management and weight.
However, the success of this system will rely on the autonomy of the navigation, secure communications, good human machine teaming and the ability to work in an electronic warfare environment. Overall it shows a big change in thinking for the Indian Army. The goal is to create a networked combat team between manned and unmanned platforms. The UGVs, UAVs, sensors and weaponry will all be used as an extension to the armoured vehicles.

evening.title: Theatre Commands: Why the IAF Fears Fragmentation of Air Power
evening.text:
As the debate regarding theatre integration in India continues to develop, we can see how the Army, Navy and Indian Air Force have differing perspectives on what integrated warfare actually means. Whilst some advocate for a unified approach by bringing land, sea and air assets together under one theatre, the IAF’s concern is that this would cause them to split up their limited air force.
It is important to understand that joint warfare should enhance the use of your military power. Generally speaking, the Army would need to deploy or keep their units in their allocated area of responsibility. An armour brigade cannot be moved as easily from Punjab to Rajasthan as a fighter squadron can be. A destroyer cannot be moved from being part of the Eastern Fleet to suddenly appearing off the western coast of India in a matter of hours.
They have different deployment requirements, timelines and logistical issues. This is why you have different command structures within the army and different fleets within the navy.
Aircraft however, can be redeployed between sectors. Although they do have different requirements depending on the base they are based out of, maintenance, logistics, airspace availability, range and threat, they can still be used in other areas. Fighter squadrons can be deployed from one region to help in other areas. With the use of aerial refuelling, long range munitions and sensor networks the range of their operations can be extended. The IAF’s concern isn’t just about who will be controlling their aircraft, but how difficult it would be to focus their limited number of fighting squadrons under different theatre commanders.
India only currently has 29 fighter squadrons (recent reports). If they were deployed to fixed geographic theatres it would be more difficult to focus enough power to deal with the most impactful threat.
The IAF has pushed for a ‘top down’ approach. As Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh stated in October 2026, “aircraft should not be seen as being tied to a specific region”. Using Operation Sindoor as an example, he stated that having a centralised command to allow the right assets to be allocated at the right time can aid integrated operations.
This does not mean that theatre commanders won’t have the right aircraft at the right time, it means that there needs to be a difference between allocating responsibility for a mission and fixing resources to a region. A maritime theatre will require air support to carry out maritime patrols, protect the fleet, ASW and strike capabilities. Land based theatres will also require air support for air defence, interdiction, support and striking further into enemy territory.
However, the air force does have their own missions to complete, such as gaining air superiority, striking strategic targets, air defence and multi theatre operations.
By splitting them too much between geographic regions, we may lose some of our capability to run a coherent air campaign across multiple fronts. During a crisis in one sector we may need to move our air assets from another region. Even if the theatre commander in the sector has competing requirements. We shouldn’t be against the idea of theatre commands or keeping things as they are. By having a joint plan, shared intel, interoperable communication and clear command links we can improve collaboration between the services.
The key will be to create a structure that recognises the differences between land, maritime and air. The theatre commander should have the authority and support required to complete their objectives. However, the national air command should have the authority to allocate our limited air assets as needed.
Overall, whilst we do need jointness in India, it doesn’t necessarily mean we need to fix assets from each service into geographic regions.

evening.title: Quad Members Reaffirm Commitment to a Free and Open Indo-Pacific
evening.text:
The Quad foreign ministers on Saturday expressed “grave concern” over “economic coercion” through arbitrary export restrictions and practices that disrupt global supply chains.
In an apparent reference to China, the foreign ministers of India, the US, Australia and Japan expressed grave concerns regarding economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions, as well as non-market policies and practices that result in overcapacity, disrupting global supply chains in critical industries.
In a joint statement after their meeting in Atlanta, the Quad foreign ministers reiterated their commitment to building reliable and open global supply chains and trusted and resilient infrastructure.
The Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting was convened by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and was attended by External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.
The ministers recognised the importance of critical sea lanes, the uninterrupted flow of commerce, energy security, and the unhindered passage and safety of maritime crews and vessels without the imposition of tolls.
They also reiterated the absolute necessity to protect and preserve navigational rights and freedoms in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in accordance with international law as reflected in UNCLOS.
This was the third Quad Foreign Ministers Meeting held this year. Earlier, the ministers met in New Delhi in May and in Manila in July.
Moves are underway to convene a Quad Leaders’ Summit, hosted by US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the ASEAN-East Asian Summits in mid-November.

evening.title: India’s TEDBF Could Offer More Than Rafale M
evening.text:
India’s Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF) was designed to meet the Indian Navies needs for a carrier based fighter, taking into account the ski-jump launch and arrested recovery capabilities, as well as the size constraints of INS Vikrant and INS Vikramaditya. While the Rafale Marine provides a capable combat proven carrier fighter to the Indian Navy, it has shown the trade-offs that have been made to fit it onto the carriers.
This is an important distinction to make between the short term need for the Indian Navy to have modern fighters in service, alongside the long term goal of developing an indigenous carrier combat aircraft.
The Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF) is to be developed by the Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) as a multi-role twin engine fighter for the Indian Navy. With a canard delta wing, folding tips, strengthened landing gear and arresting hook, the aircraft will be designed to operate from STOBAR carriers.
By designing the aircraft around these requirements from the beginning, Indian engineers will have greater flexibility in designing an aircraft with fuel, weapons, carrier compatibility and future upgrade capabilities. It will also be designed with indigenous weapons and systems, giving greater control over the future of the aircraft.
It is reported to have a max take-off weight of around 26 tonnes. There have been claims that this aircraft will have a greater payload capacity of 7.5 tonnes, compared to around 5.5 tonnes of the Rafale M. However, this is referring to the maximum external payload of the aircraft. The actual weapon payload of the aircraft during take-off from the ski-jump will depend on a number of factors such as the amount of fuel carried, the mission profile and the launch conditions. The Rafale M is not an inappropriate choice for the Indian carriers. It has been designed for naval operations, with strengthened landing gear and arresting hook. It has also been tested for use from the ski-jump.
However, when fitting it onto the INS Vikrant issues have been found due to its large wingspan of around 10.9 metres, compared to the aircraft lifts of around 10 metres on the carrier. The Navy are looking into ways to modify and operate the aircraft. Additionally the aircraft lacks foldable wings making it more difficult to move around the hangars, compared to the MiG-29K.
Overall, these are just integration issues and the Rafale M would have been a good option to provide a short term solution.
However, concerns have been raised by those wanting an indigenous aircraft, that if the TEDBF isn’t approved, funded and developed in a timely manner, the short term purchase may become a long term replacement. As of July 2026, it has been reported that the programme is still waiting for approval from the Cabinet Committee on Security. The timescale for development and prototyping will depend on the decision.
The Navy have stated in the long term, this aircraft is part of their plan for sovereign carrier aviation. In an Interview in May 2026, the Navy Chief Admiral Dinesh K. Tripathi said: “Rafale Marine is a short term solution…TEDBF is an essential step towards an indigenous solution.”
Ultimately the question is not whether the Rafale M should have been purchased as an urgent solution, but whether India can prevent this undermining the need for a national fighter. TEDBF will take many years to test and will require significant investment, but will give the opportunity to design an aircraft specifically for Indian carrier operations, with indigenous weapons and for the future needs of the Navy.

evening.title: Russian Think Tank Urges India to Buy 500 Su-57 Fighters
evening.text:
Russia has recommended that India purchase 50 Su-57 fifth generation jets and move forward with a local production deal for the remaining 450 units, with the research organisation criticising India’s Rafale and Tejas programmes. It said that New Delhi risks being left behind by China and Pakistan.
The Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade (CAWAT), created a report that was published in Russia’s National Defense magazine, stating that India needs to re-evaluate its fighter jet procurement strategy. This includes using the Su-57E as a short term solution. However, the report recommends that India should purchase 500 Su-57’s. The report states that by 2030, China will have hundreds of J-20 and J-35 units ready for deployment, whilst Pakistan will have at least 40 J-35AE units. This will leave India’s current jet fleet with a significant technological gap.
This is based on projected figures from CAWAT. The report also claimed that Rafale and Tejas simply cannot match the capabilities of China’s stealth jets.
India could purchase 50 initial units from Russia and produce a further 450 locally through licence manufacture, CAWAT said. Technology transfer could also be carried out to help develop India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft.
However, this would require significant investment, manufacturing facilities and long term funding. There is currently no evidence to suggest that India has agreed to this. The report questioned the cost of purchasing Rafale jets from France and said that India should look to increase the number of Su-30MKI jets that are currently produced via licence manufacture by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.
The report also criticised the Tejas programme as having suffered from delays, low quantities and limitations. Naval variants also did not meet the requirements of the Indian navy. This shows that India needs to re-evaluate its spending on locally developed aircraft.
These conclusions are based on the report. Different aircraft have different goals and requirements. The AMCA is planned to be India’s indigenous fifth generation fighter. Russia has been pushing the Su-57E to India often, offering licence manufacture. In January 2026, Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation stated that technical talks were underway for potential production in India. However there is no evidence to suggest that India will go ahead with this.
India has also stated that they are hesitant. Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said in September 2026 that there had been no decision made on purchasing a foreign fifth generation jet and that the AMCA is currently India’s programme.
Overall this shows the difficulties that India faces when planning their defence. They need to address the lack of fighter squadrons, prepare for China’s increasing air capabilities but also continue to develop their stealth aircraft.

evening.title: 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50
evening.text:
No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab.

Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more:

"How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement."

There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for "Editing MACroS", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy died earlier this year at the age of 83.

The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs. It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge).

As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976. (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.)

This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says:

"RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet."

RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development.

Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs, last updated in 2020.

Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008, RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August.

Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an essay called In the Beginning… Was the Command Line. (It was later republished as a rather short book, but the text is still online.) In it, he says:

"In the GNU/Linux world there are two major text editing programs: the minimalist vi (known in some implementations as elvis) and the maximalist emacs. I use emacs, which might be thought of as a thermonuclear word processor. It was created by Richard Stallman; enough said. It is written in Lisp, which is the only computer language that is beautiful. It is colossal, and yet it only edits straight ASCII text files, which is to say, no fonts, no boldface, no underlining. In other words, the engineer-hours that, in the case of Microsoft Word, were devoted to features like mail merge, and the ability to embed feature-length motion pictures in corporate memoranda, were, in the case of emacs, focused with maniacal intensity on the deceptively simple-seeming problem of editing text. If you are a professional writer–i.e., if someone else is getting paid to worry about how your words are formatted and printed–emacs outshines all other editing software in approximately the same way that the noonday sun does the stars."

Emacs is 50-plus-year-old software, and it shows. This is a huge and complicated program: decades ago, the joke was that EMACS stood for "Eight Megs And Constantly Swapping". It is not an easy program to learn. Despite lavish documentation and a built-in tutorial, this is software so old that its terminology predates microprocessors and the personal computer.

Its exhaustive manual is 804 pages long, and to pick some trivial examples, its terms for parts of the screen use “frame” to mean what’s now called a window, and “window” to mean what’s now called a pane. In the section on Keys, it discusses the Control and Meta keys. That’s a slight snag: you don’t have a Meta key, and neither do the authors of Emacs. It was a key on the now almost legendarily rare Space Cadet Keyboard, of which the Deskthority keyboard wiki says:

“It is known as the holy grail of keyboards.”

You can buy a modern replica, the Keymacs keyboard. They are hand-made in the Czech Republic, and depending on exactly what model and specifications you want, they cost from €2,998 for the Lispsaver up to €6,878 for the A624N Space Cadet.

In other words, you can have a keyboard with a real Meta key if you want, but it is going to cost you.

One of the problems with these historical terms, unfamiliar to anyone who wasn’t already programming in the 1970s, is that meanings drift. In the context of Emacs, "Meta" means Alt, or Opt on Macs. However, KDE also uses the Meta key – but what the KDE documentation calls "Meta" is the Windows key – or Command on Macs. Like most Linux folks, the GNOME documentation calls it the Super key.

Names are important. They matter. Who's right, the Emacs folks or the KDE folks? Well, neither: nobody has Meta keys any more. We have Ctrl, Alt, and Cmd/Super/Windows.

There have been valiant efforts to modernize Emacs and bring it into line with modern UI and terminology. This vulture tried to learn Aquamacs, which modernized Emacs with a native macOS UI, but sadly it's no longer maintained.

Another, which we enjoyed trying, is ErgoEmacs, which changes the key bindings and rearranges the UI into something much more like the IBM Common User Access arrangement, as used in Windows and most Linux desktops. However, it never really caught on and you need to know your way around Emacs to install it and configure it for your regional keyboard layout.

So complex is it to configure Emacs that there are multiple pre-configured distributions of Emacs, such as Doom Emacs, or the minimalist Emacs Solo. We wish someone did a "CUA-Macs" config, with ErgoEmacs integrated and able to pick up your existing keyboard config.

Come to that, the Gershwin Desktop project that we mentioned along with GhostBSD last year is in active development, and it's based around GNUstep. Maybe its developers could pick up Aquamacs, and adapt it to GNUstep.

There is a long history of such Emacs facelifts. One instance is Borland’s Sprint word-processor, one of the selling points of which was that it could emulate the user interfaces of most of the leading MS-DOS word-processors of its day (just before they all converged on IBM CUA). Before Borland acquired it, Sprint was called The Final Word, developed by musical equipment makers Mark of the Unicorn. FinalWord was based on an Emacs clone called MINCE.

The Great Rival

Another well-known Emacs distribution is Spacemacs, which adapts Emacs to have a more Vi-like user interface.

Vi is the other seminal Unix text editor, as the Stephenson quote above mentions. As this article on Origins and the Evolution of Vi & Vim notes, it too dates back to 1976. Indeed, that’s the reason we chose the year in this story: Tilde, a text editor that doesn’t work like it’s 1976. One feature of Tilde we enjoy is that it supports use of the mouse even on the Linux console – which is the headline new feature of GNU Emacs 31.1.

Vi is very much alive and well today. GNU Emacs is based on the original source code, but Vi mainly survives as re-implementations. The recreation Stephenson mentions, Elvis, lives on today in the form of nvi.

However, by far the best known is Vim, maintained by Bram Moolenaar until his death in 2023. In the grand FOSS forking tradition, it too has forks, including Neovim, as used in Omarchy, and more recently, the AI-free Vim Classic – a new project led by Drew DeVault, who just launched the similarly LLM-free AlpineBSD. ®
evening.summary:
No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab.

Landline phones will switch off across Britland in 100 days, no extensions – Openreach
evening.text:
Openreach has issued a stark reminder to customers that the legacy phone network is being officially switched off on January 31, and says the deadline will not be postponed.

The infrastructure arm of BT Group, Britain’s biggest telecoms biz, circulated the warning this week in a letter to comms providers that use its network to deliver their services.

It informs them that any customers still on legacy public switched telephone network (PSTN) connections are at risk of disruption when these are retired at the end of January, 2027.

The switch-off could affect businesses and consumers alike. Beyond the plain old telephone, systems that rely on PSTN connectivity include point-of-sale terminals, fire and security alarms, and personal care alarms for elderly and vulnerable people.

The move is part of a wider government scheme to get the UK onto all-digital high-speed networks running on fiber-optic infrastructure, and the legacy phone service – with its dependency on copper cabling – was standing in the way.

Many households have now ditched landline handsets and instead use only mobile phones, yet for those who still want a landline, the changeover means plugging the phone into the back of a broadband router to access a Digital Voice service.

Openreach has been planning this move for the best part of a decade. It has already pushed back the deadline at least once, after the government asked telecoms providers not to force vulnerable customers who use phone-network systems such as TeleCare to switch until fixes are in place.

Nevertheless, public awareness seems low that analog phone services will soon be disconnected. "Openreach and all providers need to coordinate a much more cohesive campaign that reaches customers directly," said telecoms analyst Paolo Pescatore at PP Foresight.

"TV, billboards and newspaper advertising should reinforce a consistent message, supported by targeted letters, calls and door-to-door support for older and vulnerable people who need extra help," he told The Register.

"Customers need to understand what is changing, what action to take, and who will help them. Providers must take responsibility for ensuring people remain safely connected, especially those who rely on their landline or a care alarm."

Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, agreed.

"With only three months to go, the digital landline switchover is entering a critical final phase. Most people have moved over without major problems, but nobody who relies on their landline or TeleCare should be left behind," she told us.

"Anyone with concerns should contact their provider, but the responsibility cannot rest with customers alone. Providers must not give up on people who have not responded. They need to keep trying to reach them and offer practical, individual support, recognizing that some may be unwell, living with dementia, worried about scams or without anyone nearby to help."

Openreach has a webpage with information regarding the switch-off. This advises consumers to call their service provider as soon as possible to ensure service is not interrupted.

The company previously told The Register that customers without a fiber connection will likely be switched to SOTAP for Analog (Single Order Transitional Access Product), where equipment is installed in the local telephone exchange to allow them to continue to use their old phone line as before.

Openreach has warned that commercial customers delaying migration risk significant disruption and unnecessary costs - leaving it until the last minute could make it harder to secure the requisite engineering support before the deadline hits.

"Businesses and organizations that delay action are making things harder for themselves," said James Lilley, Openreach Director of All-IP.

"The straightforward migrations have largely been completed. What's left are the complex connections that underpin critical operations, requiring careful planning, supplier coordination, and thorough testing. We are urging businesses to act now, audit their remaining analog services, and work with their communications provider on a migration plan today."

Earlier this year, the firm tried to drive home the message by announcing it was stepping up its charges to service providers and companies still operating legacy business lines, who will by now be paying double the rental cost compared to last year. ®

evening.text:
Gross GST collections increased 23 per cent to over Rs 2.31 lakh crore in October, driven by strong mop-up from domestic activities and imports, according to government data released on Sunday.
Gross GST collections from domestic sales rose 16 per cent to over Rs 1.59 lakh crore, and revenues from imports climbed 42 per cent to Rs 72,246 crore.
The Rs 2.31 lakh crore collection includes Central GST mop-up of 42,935 crore, State GST of Rs 51,340 crore and Integrated GST of over Rs 1.37 lakh crore, data showed.
Goods and Services Tax (GST) refunds increased 6.5 per cent year-on-year to Rs 27,934 crore in October.
After adjusting for refunds, net GST collections rose 26 per cent to over Rs 2.03 lakh crore in October.
During April-October, gross GST collection grew 13.2 per cent to over Rs 14.77 lakh crore. Net collections rose 13 per cent to over Rs 12.69 lakh crore.
